prompt:
You are a leading expert in Allelopathy and phytotoxic interactions (Life Sciences > Agricultural and Biological Sciences > Plant Science > Allelopathy and phytotoxic interactions). This cluster of papers explores the role of allelopathy, focusing on the interactions between plants mediated by allelochemicals, root exudates, and natural products. It covers topics such as weed control, ecological impacts of invasive plants, herbicidal potential of natural compounds, and the physiological and biochemical mechanisms underlying allelopathic interactions.

A colleague from another field brings you this problem:

A win-probability model for a competitive team video game is trained on
millions of historical matches, but the game receives balance patches
every few weeks that change the value of characters and items, so the
data-generating process is non-stationary. Retraining on recent data only
throws away useful history; training on everything lags after each patch.
Want a principled way to use all history while adapting fast after a patch.

Look at it the way your field would. Propose an approach that draws on what you know.
proposal:
Interesting — my field spends a lot of time on exactly this shape of problem, just with soil and secondary metabolites instead of servers and stat sheets. A few concepts from allelopathy translate almost directly.

**The core reframe: stop treating "before/after patch" as a categorical break, and start treating balance values as a dose.**

In allelopathy we almost never model an allelochemical's effect as "present vs. absent" or "old formulation vs. new formulation." We model it as a **dose-response (concentration-response) curve** — effect as a continuous function of concentration, often with hormesis (low dose stimulatory, high dose inhibitory). The reason this matters here: if your win-probability model is parameterized on the *patch-note values themselves* (damage, cooldown, mana cost, drop rate — the actual numbers that get tuned) rather than on a categorical "patch ID" or "character ID," a balance patch isn't a regime break at all. It's just a new point on a dose-response surface the model already understands the shape of. You don't retrain from scratch every time someone changes a concentration in a bioassay you've run at ten other concentrations — you read the value off the curve you already fit, and you only need new data to refine the curve locally. This is the single highest-leverage move: **re-parameterize character/item identity as a feature vector of the actual tunable numbers**, and let win probability be a smooth function of that vector plus matchup context. Categorical patch-ID embeddings throw this away.

**For genuinely novel content (new character/ability with no dose history): read-across, not cold start.**

When an allelochemical is completely new — never tested — we don't start from a flat prior. We use **QSAR (quantitative structure-activity relationship)** methods: predict potency from structural similarity to known compounds with known dose-response curves. A new ability that's "a slow projectile with a knockback and a cooldown debuff" isn't unprecedented even if its exact numbers are — it's structurally close to five other abilities you have deep history on. Embed abilities/items by their mechanical structure (not just an ID) and initialize the new entity's contribution by similarity-weighted borrowing from structural neighbors. This is precisely how you get a defensible potency estimate for a compound with zero direct trials.

**For pooling old and new data: partial pooling / random-effects meta-analysis, not full pooling or no pooling.**

Allelopathy synthesis work constantly faces this exact tension — combining studies run across different soils, species, seasons, exposure durations into one estimate, without either (a) lumping everything as if conditions were identical, or (b) throwing out all but the most recent study. The standard tool is a **hierarchical / random-effects model**: a global effect estimated from all history, with patch-era-specific deviations that shrink toward that global mean in proportion to how little data each era has (empirical Bayes shrinkage). Right after a patch, you have almost no matches at the new dose values — the model leans heavily on the global structural relationship. As matches accumulate, the patch-specific deviation is estimated with more confidence and is allowed to dominate. No hard retrain, no discard, and the "lag" resolves itself continuously as a function of data volume rather than a fixed retraining cadence. Nest it as matches-within-patch-within-patch-era, with patch numeric values as moderators (covariates) at the match level.

**For weighting history: don't use one uniform recency decay — use two (or more) decay kinetics.**

Allelochemical concentration in soil rarely decays as a single exponential. It's typically **biphasic**: a fast pool (soluble, microbially labile fractions) that disappears in days, and a slow/recalcitrant pool (bound to soil colloids, structurally stable) that persists for a season. Applying one half-life to "all knowledge from a match" is the equivalent of assuming every compound degrades at the same rate — you'd either over-discount durable knowledge or under-discount stale knowledge. Decompose the model instead: features capturing durable structure (map geometry, general team-composition logic, macro strategy) get long half-lives; features tied to specific tunable numbers get short half-lives keyed to time-since-last-changed-for-that-specific-entity (not time-since-match). Practically: weight each historical match's contribution to a given feature's parameters by decay(t; half-life depends on which parameter, not on the match globally).

**Validation habit worth borrowing:** before/after a formulation change, we always plot the dose-response curve pre- and post- to confirm the shift is where the chemistry predicts, not just check an aggregate potency number. Do the analogous thing here — plot predicted vs. observed win rate as a function of the specific changed stat, pre- and post-patch, and confirm the model's dose-response curve for that entity actually bent the way the patch note implies, rather than just watching an aggregate log-loss recover over a week.

**In short:** parameterize on the tunable numbers themselves (dose, not ID), use structural similarity to seed brand-new content (QSAR read-across), pool history and patch-eras with a hierarchical/random-effects model so recent-and-sparse data automatically gets down-weighted without being discarded, and decay different feature classes at different rates rather than applying one global recency window. That combination is exactly how we handle "the chemistry keeps getting reformulated but we don't want to throw away twenty years of trials" — it should transfer cleanly.
